passage:
Monday. Nilesh came back from his design jury, where the panel had marked him down for "lack of originality" on a project he'd spent a month on. Twenty minutes later the food delivery arrived late, and he snapped at the rider, "Can't you people do one simple job?" The rider left without a word. Gurleen, his flatmate, kept quiet, though she winced.
Tuesday. Over chai, Gurleen said gently, "Yesterday wasn't really about the noodles, was it? That jury sounded unfair."
Nilesh stared into his cup. "No. It wasn't."
Saturday. When the same rider came again, Nilesh handed over a tip and said, "Sorry about Monday. Bad day. Not your fault."

qa.q: What did the design panel mark Nilesh down for?
qa.a: Lack of originality.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh snap at the rider over a late delivery?
qa.a: Nilesh was stung by the unfair jury but couldn't answer the panel, so the anger spilled onto the rider, who seemed safer to blame.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen wait until Tuesday to say something?
qa.a: Correcting Nilesh in the heat of the moment might have made him defensive; a quiet remark over chai the next day let him see the real cause.

qa.q: What might Monday's delivery have been like for the rider?
qa.a: The rider was probably hurt and embarrassed to be yelled at over a delay, and left carrying someone else's bad day.

grounding: Over a week a flatmate watches a friend lash out at a delivery rider after an unfair jury, and a quiet word the next day helps him see why.

passage:
Tarun, you asked why I didn't jump on you when you shouted at the courier boy this morning. Let me tell you about my flatmate Suresh, back in 1994.
Our professor gave him a C in the viva, a grade everyone knew was unfair. That evening the tiffin man was late, and Suresh shouted at him in the corridor, called him useless. I stood there and kept my mouth shut.
Next morning, while we were getting ready for class, I said, "That viva was rotten. You were angry at the prof, not at Ramu bhai." Suresh put down his comb. He went and apologised to Ramu before class.
So, Tarun. How did your appraisal go yesterday? Your old colleague Nilesh is listening.

qa.q: What grade did Suresh get in the viva?
qa.a: A C.

qa.q: Why did Suresh shout at the tiffin man?
qa.a: Suresh was angry about the unfair viva grade but couldn't hit back at the professor, so the anger landed on the late tiffin man, who was within reach.

qa.q: Why did young Nilesh wait until the next morning to speak?
qa.a: In the corridor, correcting Suresh would likely have made him defensive; a quiet word the next morning named the real target and let him choose to apologise.

qa.q: How might Tarun take the question about the appraisal?
qa.a: Tarun may feel caught out but also understood, realising Nilesh has guessed that the courier wasn't the real problem.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls how, as a student, a quiet remark the morning after helped a flatmate see his outburst at the tiffin man was about an unfair viva.

passage:
Rain had flooded half of Koramangala, the lift was out, and the grocery delivery was forty minutes late. Jeevan had just read his internship review, "Needs more initiative", from a manager who had never once answered his emails. When the soaked delivery man finally climbed four floors with the bags, Jeevan snapped, "Forty minutes! Do you even know how to read a map?"
Anirban, his flatmate, didn't argue in the doorway. He took the bags, thanked the man twice and handed him a towel.
Later, once the power came back, Anirban said quietly, "That review was unfair. The delivery guy climbed four floors in a flood, though."
Jeevan was silent a long time. Then he picked up his phone and left the man a note: "Sorry. Thank you."

qa.q: What did Jeevan's internship review say?
qa.a: "Needs more initiative."

qa.q: Why did Jeevan snap at the delivery man?
qa.a: Jeevan felt the review was unfair but couldn't challenge the manager right then, so the frustration came out at the soaked delivery man, an easier target.

qa.q: Why was Anirban's choice to stay quiet in the doorway wise?
qa.a: Arguing then might have made Jeevan defend himself; kindness to the delivery man first and a quiet remark later let Jeevan see the real source and make amends.

qa.q: What was the evening like for the delivery man?
qa.a: He climbed four floors in a flood and was insulted at the door, though Anirban's towel and thanks softened it a little.

grounding: In a flooded city with the lift out, a flatmate sees a friend lash out at a delivery man after an unfair review and speaks quietly about it later.

passage:
Karthik came back from the lab viva with his jaw set. The examiner had given him six out of twenty after asking three questions from a chapter that wasn't even in the syllabus. Asif, his flatmate in their Guindy rental, had heard the whole story on the stairs.
An hour later the dinner order came, with the wrong curry. Karthik yanked the door open. "Can't you read? Is it that hard?" The delivery man, sweat on his forehead, just stared.
Asif stepped in, thanked the man, and handed him a small tip. He said nothing to Karthik then.
Late that night, on the terrace, Asif passed him a cup of tea. "That wasn't really about the curry, was it?"
Karthik let out a long breath. "No. It was that viva." He rubbed his face. "I'll say sorry next time he comes."

qa.q: What mark did the examiner give Karthik in the viva?
qa.a: The examiner gave him six out of twenty.

qa.q: What does Asif's silence at the door suggest about what he was thinking?
qa.a: Asif seemed to think that correcting Karthik in the heat of the moment would only add fuel, so he settled things with the delivery man first and saved his words for later.

qa.q: Why did Asif's quiet question on the terrace work better than a scolding at the door?
qa.a: By then Karthik had cooled down, and naming the viva as the real cause let him see it himself and decide to apologise.

qa.q: How might the delivery man have felt when Karthik shouted at him?
qa.a: He had only brought an order he didn't cook, so he was likely stunned and hurt; Asif's thanks and tip may have softened it a little.

grounding: Shows a flatmate who sees a friend snap at a delivery man after an unfair viva and, instead of correcting him then, later names what really happened.

passage:
"Farhan, your groceries are here."
"Finally." He took the bags and peered in. "Where's the paneer? You people can't even pack a list?"
"Sir, it was out of stock, it says on the—"
"Of course it does." Door shut.
Ganga looked up from her laptop. Farhan stood holding the bag, breathing hard. She said nothing and went back to her spreadsheet.
Later, over rice and dal on the sofa of their shared flat:
"That internship presentation today... they really wrote 'below expectations'?"
"After I did half the team's slides. Yeah."
"That sounds unfair. I think it's still sitting in you."
Farhan put his spoon down. "I yelled at a guy about paneer."
"You did."
"It wasn't the paneer."
"Nope."
"Next time I order, I'm adding a sorry note for him."

qa.q: Which item was missing from Farhan's groceries?
qa.a: The paneer; it was out of stock.

qa.q: Why might Ganga have stayed quiet when Farhan shut the door?
qa.a: She seemed to judge that pointing it out right then would make Farhan defensive, and she guessed the real sting was the presentation, not the groceries.

qa.q: What made Ganga's later remark land well?
qa.a: She waited until they were calm over dinner, named the unfair review as the likely cause, and let Farhan reach the conclusion himself.

qa.q: What might the delivery person have taken away from the doorstep?
qa.a: The delivery person was blamed for stock they didn't control and cut off mid-sentence, so they may have felt belittled and brushed aside.

grounding: Illustrates a flatmate who watches a friend lash out at a delivery person after an unfair internship review and helps more with a quiet remark later than with a correction at the door.
